title: Punctuation & Capitalisation
description: Learn punctuation for Grade 6: full stop, comma, question and exclamation marks, apostrophe, inverted commas, capital letters, plus an intro to colon and semicolon — with practice and tests.

topics.title: End Marks, Commas & the Apostrophe
topics.concept:
End marks close a sentence: full stop (.) for statements and commands, question mark (?) for questions, exclamation mark (!) for strong feeling.

The comma (,) shows a short pause. Use it:

  • between items in a list: I bought pens, books and a bag.
  • after an introductory word: Yes, I agree. However, it was late.
  • to address someone: Ravi, come here.

The apostrophe (') has two jobs:

  • Possession: Ram's book; the girls' school.
  • Contraction (missing letters): do not → don't; it is → it's.

examples.problem: Add commas: I need eggs milk bread and butter.
examples.solution: I need eggs, milk, bread and butter. — commas separate items in a list.
they're — the apostrophe replaces the missing 'a' of 'are'.

topics.title: Inverted Commas, Capital Letters & Intro to Colon/Semicolon
topics.concept:
Inverted commas (" ") mark the exact words someone speaks. Put the spoken words inside, with the end punctuation inside too: "I am ready," she said.

Capital letters are used for:

  • the first word of a sentence;
  • the pronoun I;
  • proper nouns: names, places, days, months, festivals (Ravi, Delhi, Monday, July, Diwali);
  • the main words in titles.

Colon (:) introduces a list or explanation: Bring these: a pen, a ruler and an eraser. A semicolon (;) joins two closely related sentences: It was late; we went home.

examples.problem: Punctuate the speech: i am coming said ravi
examples.solution: "I am coming," said Ravi. — capital I and Ravi, comma inside the quotes, full stop at the end.

examples.problem: Which words need capitals? on monday we visit my uncle in jaipur.
examples.solution: On Monday we visit my uncle in Jaipur. — first word, day 'Monday', and place 'Jaipur'.

recap: Inverted commas hold the exact spoken words
Capitals: sentence start, 'I', proper nouns, titles
Colon introduces a list; semicolon joins related sentences

questions.q: Which end mark suits 'Are you coming'?
questions.explanation: It is a question → '?'.
'I'm' = I am.
'India' is a proper noun.

I like, tea coffee and milk.

questions.explanation: Commas separate list items.
Singular possessive → 'boy's'.
An exclamation takes '!'.
Comma inside the quotes, then 'he said'.

questions.q: Punctuate correctly: 'the teacher said do your homework'
options: The teacher said do your homework.
questions.explanation: Comma before the quote, capital 'Do', end mark inside the quotes.

questions.q: Choose the sentence with correct apostrophe use.
questions.explanation: 'children' is already plural, so add 's: children's.

questions.q: Identify the error: 'My friend, who lives in Goa is visiting us.'
questions.explanation: A non-defining clause needs commas on both sides: '…, who lives in Goa, is…'.

questions.q: Which sentence uses the semicolon correctly?
options: It was raining; so we stayed in.
It was raining; we stayed in.
It was raining, we stayed in;
It was raining; and we stayed in.
questions.explanation: A semicolon joins two related independent clauses without a conjunction.

questions.q: Capitalise correctly: 'on republic day, we sang the national anthem.'
options: On Republic Day, we sang the National Anthem.
On republic day, we sang the national anthem.
On Republic day, we sang the National anthem.
on Republic Day, we sang the national anthem.
questions.explanation: Proper nouns 'Republic Day' and the title 'National Anthem' are capitalised.

options: You will need: a pen, a ruler and an eraser.
You will need a pen: a ruler and an eraser.
You: will need a pen, a ruler and an eraser.
You will: need a pen, a ruler and an eraser.
questions.explanation: The colon follows a complete clause and introduces the list.

questions.q: Rearrange and punctuate: 'said / where / are / you / she / going'
options: Where are you going she said?
Where are you going, she said.
questions.explanation: Question mark inside the quotes, then 'she said'.

questions.q: Which option fixes the run-on? 'I was tired I went to bed.'
options: I was tired, I went to bed.
I was tired; I went to bed.
I was tired I, went to bed.
I was, tired I went to bed.
questions.explanation: A semicolon (or a full stop) correctly joins two independent clauses.

outcomes: Use the full stop, question mark and exclamation mark correctly
Place commas in lists and after introductory words
Use the apostrophe for possession and contractions

intro.en: Punctuation marks are the traffic signals of writing. They tell the reader when to pause, stop, or show feeling. Without them, sentences become confusing. Compare: "Let's eat, Grandma!" and "Let's eat Grandma!" — one comma changes everything.
intro.hi: विराम-चिह्न (Punctuation) लेखन के यातायात-संकेत हैं। ये पाठक को बताते हैं कि कब रुकना है, ठहरना है या भाव दिखाना है। इनके बिना वाक्य उलझ जाते हैं। तुलना करें: "Let's eat, Grandma!" और "Let's eat Grandma!" — एक अल्पविराम सब कुछ बदल देता है।

real_life.situation:
You write a quick note:

Note: Riya, please buy apples, bananas, and milk. Don't forget Dad's medicine!
real_life.why: The comma after 'Riya' addresses her; the commas separate the list; the apostrophe in 'Don't' marks a contraction and in 'Dad's' shows possession; the exclamation mark adds urgency. Each mark has a clear job.

reading.passage: "Hurry up, Aman!" called his mother. "We're already late." Aman grabbed his bag, his water bottle and his lunch box. "I'm ready, Mum," he said. They left the house on Tuesday morning and reached Ria's school by eight.

questions.q: Why is there a comma in 'Hurry up, Aman!'?
questions.answer: The comma separates the command from the name being addressed (Aman).

questions.q: What does the apostrophe in 'We're' show?
questions.answer: A contraction of 'We are' — the apostrophe marks the missing 'a'.

questions.q: Name two words capitalised because they are proper nouns.
questions.answer: Aman and Ria (also 'Tuesday', 'Mum') — names and the day.

challenge.q: Where does the comma change the meaning? 'Let's eat ___ Grandma.'
options: A comma after 'eat' shows we are inviting Grandma to eat
challenge.explanation: 'Let's eat, Grandma' addresses her; without the comma it sounds like eating Grandma!

challenge.q: Punctuate correctly: 'i have three pets a dog a cat and a fish'
options: I have three pets: a dog, a cat and a fish.
I have three pets a dog a cat and a fish.
I have three pets; a dog a cat and a fish.
i have three pets, a dog, a cat and a fish.
challenge.explanation: A colon introduces the list, commas separate the items, capital 'I' to start.
